name: ARC (AI2 Reasoning Challenge)
description: A dataset of 7,787 natural, grade-school science questions partitioned into a Challenge Set (2,590 questions answered incorrectly by both retrieval-based and word co-occurrence algorithms) and an Easy Set (5,197 questions). The dataset is designed to encourage AI research in advanced question answering requiring knowledge and reasoning beyond surface-level cues.
creator: Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence
citeAs: Peter Clark, Isaac Cowhey, Oren Etzioni, Tushar Khot, Ashish Sabharwal, Carissa Schoenick, Oyvind Tafjord. Think you have Solved Question Answering? Try ARC, the AI2 Reasoning Challenge. arXiv:1803.05457v1 [cs.AI] 14 Mar 2018
rai:dataCollection: Questions were collected through extensive search and investigation over several months from various standardized test sources including state assessments, national assessments, and international assessments. The dataset consists of questions authored for human standardized tests across multiple US states and educational programs.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Questions were drawn from multiple standardized test sources including: Arkansas Comprehensive Testing Assessment and Accountability Program (ACTAAP), Arizona's Instrument to Measure Standards (AIMS), Alaska Department of Education & Early Development, California Standards Test, Florida Comprehensive Assessment Test (FCAT), Louisiana Department of Education, Maryland School Assessment, Massachusetts Comprehensive Assessment System (MCAS), Maine Educational Assessment (MEA), Michigan Educational Assessment Program (MEAP), Mercury (anonymous content partner), New York State Educational Department Regents exams, Ohio Achievement Tests, Texas Assessment of Knowledge and Skills (TAKS), TIMSS assessments (1995, 2003, 2007, 2011), Virginia Standards of Learning, Washington Assessment of Student Learning (WASL), and others. Questions target grade levels 3-9 (students typically age 8-13 years).
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The dataset was partitioned into a Challenge Set and an Easy Set. Challenge questions were operationally defined as those answered incorrectly by both an Information Retrieval (IR) solver and a Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI) solver. The IR solver searches for explicit statements of question+answer in a corpus (Waterloo corpus, 51010 tokens, 280GB). The PMI solver measures strength of associations between question n-grams and answer option n-grams using pointwise mutual information within a 10-word window.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Questions were filtered to include only non-diagram, multiple-choice questions (typically 4-way multiple choice). The dataset was partitioned into train/dev/test splits. Challenge Set: 1119 train, 299 dev, 1172 test. Easy Set: 2251 train, 570 dev, 2376 test. Questions vary in length from 2 to 128 words (average 22.3 for Challenge, 19.4 for Easy), with 1 to 11 sentences per question. Answer options vary from 1 to 39 words (average 4.9 for Challenge, 3.7 for Easy).
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Questions were originally authored by human test developers for standardized tests. No additional annotation was performed for the ARC dataset beyond the original test authorship. Correct answers were provided as part of the original test materials.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset contains only non-diagram multiple-choice questions, excluding questions that require visual reasoning. Questions are limited to grade-school science topics (grades 3-9). The Challenge Set partition is defined operationally based on failure of two specific baseline algorithms (IR and PMI), which only approximates the informal goal of identifying 'hard' questions. From vocabulary analysis, only 11 question words (mainly proper nouns) do not appear in the accompanying ARC Corpus. The dataset focuses on English language questions from US educational standards.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is designed for training, testing, and validation of question answering systems that require advanced reasoning and knowledge beyond surface-level cues. Specific use cases include: developing systems that can perform multi-hop reasoning, handle questions requiring commonsense knowledge, process questions involving various knowledge types (definitions, basic facts, structure, processes, teleology, algebraic reasoning, experiments, spatial/kinematic reasoning), and employ different reasoning strategies (question logic, linguistic matching, comparison, hypothetical/counterfactual reasoning, explanation, analogy). The dataset is partitioned into train/dev/test splits to support model development and evaluation. Systems are scored using a rubric where correct answers receive 1 point and k-way ties including the correct answer receive 1/k points.
